notes.h: Meaning of equality of opportunity (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Equality of opportunity means every student has a fair chance to access, take part in and benefit from education, whatever their background. It is about the chance, not about guaranteeing that everyone ends up with the same result.
points: Equal access means every student can enrol and attend; equal outcomes means students finish with similar results. The two are different, because equal access does not automatically lead to equal outcomes.
Every person should have a fair chance to enter, take part in and progress through education, whatever their gender, family background, income, ability, disability, ethnicity or where they live.
Students begin school from different starting points, so equal treatment alone may not give equal opportunity.
Equity means giving extra support in proportion to need, so that students at a disadvantage can reach the same level of achievement as others.

Free education helps: the State funds primary and second-level education, and the Free Fees Initiative pays third-level tuition for eligible undergraduates. Even so, some groups still have lower participation and results, so the State adds targeted supports.
Barriers to equality of opportunity include gender, socio-economic status, disability, family background and location.

The Equal Status Acts 2000 to 2018 prohibit discrimination in education, in schools, colleges and access to courses, on grounds that include gender, civil status, family status, age, disability, race, religion, sexual orientation and membership of the Traveller community. There is an exemption for single-sex schools.

The Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018 bars schools from using religion as a selection criterion when they are oversubscribed (the minority-faith-school exception remains). The Education Act 1998 sets out equality of access as a goal of the system.
notes.tip: Do not mix up equality of opportunity (a fair chance) with equality of outcome (the same result). Say clearly which one the State aims for and why extra help (equity) is still needed.

notes.h: Gender and equality of opportunity (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Gender inequity in education has changed direction over time. Girls once had fewer opportunities, but today the inequity lies mainly in the subjects students choose and the careers that follow.
points: In the past girls had fewer opportunities, for example fewer girls stayed on to the Leaving Certificate or went to third level. Today girls' participation and attainment at second and third level are, on average, higher than boys'.

Boys are more likely than girls to leave school early, to have lower literacy levels at second level and to achieve lower grades on average. Reasons include peer pressure against being seen to work hard, lower expectations and less engagement with some subjects and teaching methods.

Subject choice can be gendered: fewer girls than boys take subjects such as Physics, Engineering, Construction Studies, Technology and Design and Communication Graphics, and fewer boys take subjects such as Home Economics, Languages and Art.
Single-sex schools can limit the subjects on offer, for example a girls' school without technical subjects or a boys' school without Home Economics, so students may not get the chance to choose them.
Subject choice affects later course and career choices, which is why there are fewer women in engineering and IT and fewer men in caring and teaching roles at primary level.

Teacher and parent expectations can differ by gender, and stereotypes held by parents, teachers and peers, textbooks, career guidance and a lack of role models can influence the subjects and courses students consider.
Schools can widen opportunity by encouraging students to choose subjects on the basis of ability and interest rather than gender stereotypes.

Other responses include less stereotyped textbooks and resources, mixed-gender access to subjects, encouragement into non-traditional subjects (for example promoting STEM for girls), gender balance in career guidance and equality legislation.
notes.tip: A strong answer gives gender inequity as a statement with evidence, then a response: for example girls often attain more than boys and boys are more likely to leave early, and subject choice depends on whether the school is single-sex or co-educational. Do not claim girls are disadvantaged overall, and never explain boys' results by ability.

notes.h: Socio-economic status and equality of opportunity (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Socio-economic status (SES) is a family's position based on income, occupation and education, also called social class. It shapes a student's chances because it affects what a family can pay for, what it expects and what support it can give.
points: Students from higher groups (professional, managerial) are more likely to complete second level and go on to third level. Students from lower socio-economic groups are more likely to leave school early and less likely to progress to third level, so they are under-represented at third level.
School costs such as books, equipment, uniforms, trips, subject charges, school bags and technology, transport and, at third level, accommodation and living costs can exclude low-income families.

Partial relief comes from the back-to-school clothing and footwear allowance, book rental schemes and grants, school meals and school transport schemes, free fees and SUSI grants, and the Back to Education Allowance with its Cost of Education Allowance add-on for participants with dependent children.
These supports reduce costs, but they do not remove the wider gap in resources between families.

Higher-status families usually offer higher expectations and aspiration, more help with homework and course choices, a quiet place to study, grinds and extra-curricular activities, and social contacts and knowledge of the system, so their children start with advantages.

Parents with higher levels of education are more likely to have high expectations for their children and to be able to help with schoolwork. Lower-status families may face a cycle of poverty and low expectations, poor housing or crowding, and pressure to earn.

School factors add to this. Some schools use streaming (grouping students by ability), and students in lower-status groups may be placed in lower streams or sets, which can limit the subject level, grades and courses open to them.
Teacher expectations and the locality of a school (a disadvantaged area, with fewer resources and more early leaving) can reinforce the effects of socio-economic status.

Responses include DEIS (Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools), which gives extra support to schools in disadvantaged communities, HEAR, which gives reduced-points third-level entry to students from disadvantaged backgrounds, and the financial supports above.
notes.tip: When asked to comment on or analyse the effect of socio-economic status, make about three points, each linking a cause to an effect: for example costs exclude low-income families but allowances and grants offset them; higher-status families give more opportunity and more progression to third level; DEIS and HEAR respond.

notes.b: A disadvantaged student is one at risk of low achievement because of several causes working together, not just low income. Knowing who is at risk, what holds them back and what helps lets you answer both the short and the long questions.
points: Groups at risk of educational disadvantage include students from low-income and unemployed families, Travellers, Roma, students from migrant, asylum-seeking or refugee families, students with disabilities or special educational needs, homeless young people, young people in care, those in disadvantaged areas and lone-parent households.
Students from migrant families may need language support in English or Irish (English as an additional language), and their qualifications from other countries may not be recognised.
Students living in disadvantaged areas may face poor housing, poor health, lack of study space and limited access to after-school activities, which makes it harder to study and take part.
Other barriers are poverty, discrimination, low expectations, lack of role models and, in some communities, negative experiences of school. These lead to low attendance and early leaving.

The DEIS (Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools) programme identifies schools serving disadvantaged communities and gives them extra staffing and supports. These include the school completion programme, homework clubs, mentoring, school meals, home school community liaison and enhanced book grants.

Other responses to name are language support, learning support and special needs assistants (SNAs), Traveller and Roma education supports, grants and allowances, school meals and transport, and the Home School Community Liaison scheme.
notes.tip: For a question on equality of opportunity at second level for students at risk of disadvantage and social exclusion, give three points, each with a named scheme and what it does: for example DEIS, learning support and SNAs, language assistance and equipment, exam accommodations, or a smaller pupil-teacher ratio.

notes.b: Leaving school early closes doors that are hard to reopen. Knowing who is at risk, why students leave and what follows explains why the State invests in keeping them in school.
points: An early school leaver is a young person who leaves school before completing senior cycle, that is before the Leaving Certificate or an equivalent programme.
Early school leaving is more likely among students with poor attendance and truancy, low literacy and numeracy, or learning difficulties, because they fall behind and lose interest.
Bullying, family problems, poverty and the cost of staying on, and negative peer pressure all increase the risk of leaving school early.

Other causes are a cycle of poverty and low parental expectation, living in a disadvantaged area, dislike of school or a lack of suitable programmes, the pull of jobs, pregnancy, and health or addiction problems.
Leaving school early means few or no qualifications, which limits access to further and third-level education and training and to skilled employment.
Later in life early school leaving is linked with unemployment or low-paid unskilled work, welfare dependence, poverty, low self-esteem, poor health, social exclusion and a higher risk of crime.
The effects spread: the next generation is also affected through the cycle of poverty, and the State loses skills and pays more in welfare.

Responses include the School Completion Programme, the Home School Community Liaison scheme, DEIS, the Educational Welfare Service of Tusla (which deals with school attendance), JCSP and LCA, Youthreach, the Back to Education Allowance and VTOS.
notes.tip: Short questions ask for two reasons students leave early and two effects of leaving early. For an evaluation of two initiatives for early school leavers, name each scheme, say what it does and say whether it works.

keyTerms.definition: The principle that every student has a fair chance to access, take part in and benefit from education, regardless of background.
Providing extra support in proportion to need so that students who start at a disadvantage can reach a comparable level of achievement.
A family's social and economic position, usually based on income, occupation and education level.
A young person who leaves school before completing a senior cycle programme such as the Leaving Certificate.
The situation where a student's background, location or circumstances limit their access to education and their achievement in it.
Grouping students by ability for particular subjects or for the whole school year, which can affect the grades and courses open to them.
Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools, the Department of Education programme that gives extra supports to schools serving disadvantaged communities.
Patterns in which students choose subjects differently by gender, often reflecting stereotypes rather than ability.

questions.prompt: Outline two ways in which socio-economic status can limit equality of opportunity in education.
questions.model: Any two, three marks each: families with low incomes struggle to pay for books, equipment and uniforms and so may be excluded from full participation; parents with lower levels of education may have lower expectations and less ability to help with schoolwork; students from lower socio-economic groups are more likely to leave school early and less likely to progress to third level; placement in lower streams can limit grades and courses.

questions.prompt: Analyse how gender, socio-economic status and early school leaving affect equality of opportunity in education, referring to one initiative that responds to disadvantage.
questions.model: Gender: boys more likely to leave school early and to have lower literacy; subject choice shaped by gender stereotypes, with fewer girls in Physics and fewer boys in Home Economics. Socio-economic status: cost of books, equipment and uniforms; allowances, book rental and grants reduce but do not remove barriers; parental education and expectations; lower socio-economic groups less likely to progress to third level; streaming and teacher expectations. Early school leaving: definition as leaving before completing senior cycle; risk factors such as poor attendance, low literacy, bullying, family problems and poverty; consequences such as limited access to further and third-level education and skilled work, and later unemployment and social exclusion. Initiative: DEIS, which gives extra staffing and supports to schools in disadvantaged communities, with an explanation of how it addresses one of the barriers named.
